findings.issue: The tenant clock lock is correct inside PostgreSQL. SELECT FOR UPDATE on the tenant row is held until commit or rollback. Under READ COMMITTED the next append re-reads the latest committed value, so microsecond timestamps become strictly increasing in commit order, and a rollback also rolls back the clock. The public cursor does not keep that precision, though. EventStreamCursor.createdAt is a JS Date with millisecond resolution (packages/backend/src/event-stream/types.ts:11-14). packages/data has no setTypeParser, so pg returns timestamptz as a Date truncated to the millisecond. The service stores row.createdAt as the cursor (event-stream.service.ts:198,203,215), and the tiebreaker id is a random UUID v4. Race: T1 commits event a at 10:00:00.123400 with id 'f…'. The reader emits a, and the cursor becomes (…123, 'f…'). T2 took the lock after T1 committed and commits b at …123401 with id '1…'. If listSince compares in milliseconds, (…123, '1…') > (…123, 'f…') is false, so b is skipped for good. If listSince compares the microsecond column against the truncated Date, it re-emits a and the other rows from the same millisecond. With more than batchSize rows in one millisecond the cursor never advances (livelock). So the 1µs step does not guarantee 'sem perder evento tardio' while the cursor stays (Date, uuid-v4) and packages/backend stays unchanged.
findings.required_change: Pick one approach and prove it with two concurrent appends in the same millisecond that commit out of order. (a) Under the same lock, assign a per-tenant sequence and make the id sortable in commit order (for example UUIDv7 with a monotonic counter, or an id with a lexicographic prefix from the sequence). listSince then compares (date_trunc('milliseconds', created_at), id) with the same semantics as the Date cursor. (b) Use a 1 ms step, which is a new limit of about 1000 events/s per tenant and so needs an Owner row. (c) Change the public cursor to microseconds or a sequence, which is an SSE cursor change and needs the existing Owner row. Also require an Inspector test with more than batchSize events in one millisecond.

findings.issue: A new connection with no Last-Event-ID starts at cursor = { createdAt: source.now(scope), id: '' } (event-stream.service.ts:128,135). If the outbox adapter's now() returns clock_timestamp() or now(), a remaining race exists. T holds the clock lock with a timestamp t_T taken before the reader's now(). T commits after the reader computes now. listSince(cursor > t_T) then never returns T. The lock orders appenders among themselves but does not order the reader's initial cursor.
findings.required_change: The contract must require the outbox EventStreamSource.now(scope) to return the tenant's last committed clock value: a non-locking read of the clock row, in the same unit as the cursor. Any in-flight append then gets a strictly greater timestamp. Require a test where the reader opens between another transaction's append and its commit, and the event must be delivered.

findings.issue: The preflight keeps legacy enqueue/upsert but does not say whether those rows, or rows migrated from 0018, enter the log read by listSince. An upsert that does not take the clock lock, or that rewrites created_at, reopens the skip race. The lock also serializes every appending transaction of a tenant until commit. That acts as a concurrency limit, and it can deadlock with domain locks when the order is domain → clock in one transaction and clock → domain in another (for example the per-item OFS applier).
findings.required_change: Fix three points. Only rows written under the clock lock are visible to the cursor; legacy enqueue either does not feed the stream or takes the same lock. Migrated history gets a timestamp or sequence at or below the initial clock value. Declare the lock order (clock acquired last, just before commit, or always first) and the expected impact on per-tenant throughput, with a deadlock test.

findings.issue: 'Reivindica só seu evento pendente mais antigo' is ambiguous. If 'pendente' excludes SENT rows under lease or ERROR rows waiting for retry, event N+1 of the same aggregate can be sent while N waits for retry. Per-aggregate order is then broken. Reclaim after lease expiry also makes double delivery possible.
findings.required_change: Define that the oldest non-terminal event of the aggregate (pending, leased/SENT without a final ACK, or ERROR with a scheduled retry) blocks the later ones. State at-least-once delivery, with the idempotencyKey or eventId forwarded to the provider so it can deduplicate after a reclaim.

findings.issue: The ACK state machine allows several ACKs per event, but the preflight does not say that UNIQUE(message_id) on outbox.acknowledgements with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING has to go or change. It also does not say that the ledger/ACK tenant_id comes from the event rather than the input. Offline backfill (line 108) does not document the adopter's upgrade order.
findings.required_change: Make three things explicit. The ACK table is one row per received ACK, with a separate current-state projection. tenant_id is derived by join or through the composite FK from the event. Add an upgrade-order section for adopters of migrations/0002 in offline-sync-api.md.

summary: All seven blocking findings from cycle 1 have concrete treatment. (1) An Owner/Architect table with contracts blocked until the Owner decides. (2) Legacy enqueue plus append with an explicit key, a superseding ADR, per-aggregate dispatch, and ACK by (tenant, eventId) that fails closed for legacy ACKs. (3) A composite FK on the ledger and ACK under the owner role, a lease/reclaim, and an ACK state machine. (4) Versioned JCS that does not reuse canonicalJson. (5) Level derived from verified evidence, with mock, /mock, synthetic CMS and local time blocked. (6) Offline identity by (tenant, key) with the hash as an integrity check, plus the three proof cases. (7) Via the precision items. The five precision findings were also incorporated: batch table, sequence, receipt and resume; agent and policy ports; migration ≥0021 and offline 0002; structural indicator and injected port; CTG5 → OFS order. Nothing assumes a pending Owner decision. The tenant timestamp lock does serialize commits correctly inside PostgreSQL, but it does not prevent skipping a late append at the public cursor. The cursor is a JS Date with millisecond precision, with a random UUID v4 as the tiebreaker, so two events in the same millisecond can be skipped or re-emitted in a livelock. The initial cursor from now() can also pass a transaction that is still holding the lock. The preflight needs to choose a sortable id or sequence under the lock, a 1 ms step, or a cursor change (both of those as an Owner row), and to set now() to the last committed clock value. After that repair it can move on to drafting the conditional contracts.
